pillar_reactions.evidence: He extended the rep's point with his own mechanism rather than just accepting it: 'I started realizing the meaning of muscle memory ... your muscles got used to the repetitive things and then you're not engaging the other muscles. And that's when I realized when I was doing these different workouts that Trevor was posting. I was like, oh wait, I can feel this muscle now.' He had already sold himself on the modality before the call, describing a Trevor circuit he attempted two days earlier: 'I did that with a 30 pound kettlebell. And I did like three rounds back to back ... I was completely toasted.'

The pillar that mapped most directly onto his stated problem, and he said so: 'that's exactly what I was trying to get out of this program ... if I were to figure out all of this, that's a lot of mental cognitive effort.' He framed the value as removed decision load rather than as nutrition knowledge: 'I'm not going to spend my brain cycles on researching what I should be eating, what I should not be eating, when I should be eating, how much I should be eating. All of this is taken care. There is a plan that is given to me. I just follow it blindly.'

Understood and agreed, and played back the offer accurately without needing correction: 'you folks are gonna help with custom creating workout plans, custom creating diet plans, and then also coach along the way, getting constant feedback on how I'm doing my workouts. Can I be a little more intense? Am I using the right weights?' No questions about the app, the community or the weekly check-ins. Notably the community and group trainings — the part of the offer nearest to what he liked about his 2016 HIIT classes — drew no reaction at all.

anchors.raw: I was more prepared for like, you know, 300-ish per month. Given that it's like almost three times of what I planned for, I just need to figure out, like, how do I come up with the funds?
anchors.competitor: Peloton subscription and conventional personal training
anchors.note: The reference class is a fitness app subscription plus what a trainer costs locally, and $300/month is roughly three to four times a Peloton membership. The manager's read on this call afterwards is the sharpest framing of it in the corpus: 'that's about a $300 a month problem'. The anchor was never displaced because no cost of inaction was ever built, so $1,000/month was measured against a want rather than against a consequence.

anchors.raw: I was more thinking about like, you know, and this is all going to be virtual, right? Like this is not going to be in-person and everything is just going to be through the app.
anchors.note: The same objection that lost the Ricardo call reviewed in the 10 June team meeting — that $6,000 is steep for something delivered remotely. Here it was raised in the same breath as the price and the rep isolated the money and left the virtual-versus-in-person half entirely unanswered. Management has a taught reframe for exactly this ('does it really matter how it's done as long as you're able to get the results?') and it did not run.

anchors.raw: you're buying a really expensive watch that's going to be with you for the rest of your life. It's not like you're going and renting something. The watch is your body, in this case ... you're basically investing into your body, and that is going to be with you for the rest of your life.
anchors.note: Proposed label: prospect_generated_value_frame. The prospect built the justification himself, unprompted, and it is stronger than anything the rep offered. He then immediately undercut it — 'Are we ready to commit to that $6,000, like, today? That's the bigger question' — which is the moment the rep had an open invitation to close and did not take it.

unmet_demand.want: A lower monthly commitment around $300 rather than a lump sum or $650/month financing
unmet_demand.why_unmet: One-to-one is sold only as $6,000 for six months or $4,000 for three, and the only financing brings it to $650/month over twelve. Primal University at $199/month was never mentioned to this prospect at all, even though it sits closest to his stated budget — the one call in this batch where the downsell would have been on-target and it was not offered.

unmet_demand.want: Justification for remote coaching at a price he associates with in-person work
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He raised it explicitly and it was never answered. The programme's actual answer — form review from submitted video, 24/7 direct access, custom programming — exists and was described elsewhere in the call but was never connected back to the objection.

unmet_demand.want: An answer to whether 195-200 lb at six feet is the right target, and whether age and metabolism are now limiting him
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He asked directly — 'I'm six feet tall and I want to understand, is that like an ideal weight? Should I be dropping more weight, building more muscle?' and later wondered 'maybe it's the age, maybe it's the metabolism'. The rep deflected to how he looks rather than the scale and never returned to it. This is the question a diagnostic answer would have made the programme feel necessary rather than optional.
